abstract: Mechanically induced brain injury triggers rapid cellular responses that shape long-term neurological outcomes, yet the early evolution of functional network disruption remains poorly defined. In particular, how neuronal activity changes within seconds of deformation and whether these responses determine subsequent circuit organization remain unknown. Here, we combined controlled mechanical stretch with high-speed calcium imaging to measure neuronal calcium dynamics within seconds of injury and track the same cells over 24 hours. We identify strain- and strain-rate-dependent disruption modes, including rapid reduction of calcium transient activity under moderate loading and collapse of network bursting beyond distinct mechanical thresholds. These disruptions persist despite preserved cell viability, revealing an additional functional injury pathway. These findings show that functional impairment emerges within seconds of mechanical loading and that the severity of deformation dictates the mode of network disruption, establishing mechanical thresholds as key determinants of secondary injury progression.
